glossary.title: Al dente
glossary.short_definition: The doneness of pasta or rice cooked "to the bite," still offering a little resistance.
glossary.detailed: Al dente literally means "to the tooth." Taste about a minute before the package time is up — pasta should offer a slight resistance, never be soft to the point of falling apart.

glossary.title: Soffritto
glossary.short_definition: The base of many Italian dishes: onion, carrot, and celery, slowly sautéed together.
glossary.detailed: The three vegetables are finely diced and slowly sautéed in oil or butter until translucent — the base of countless Italian sauces, risottos, and stocks.

glossary.title: Blanching
glossary.short_definition: Briefly scalding vegetables or fruit in boiling water, then cooling them quickly in an ice bath.
glossary.detailed: Vegetables are briefly boiled to keep their color and crunch, then plunged straight into ice water to stop the cooking. Also used for peeling tomatoes.
glossary.usage: Rajčata, mandle, zelené fazolky, brokolice před dalším zpracováním.

glossary.title: Poaching
glossary.short_definition: Gentle cooking in hot but not boiling liquid, usually water, stock, or milk.
glossary.detailed: The temperature is held just below boiling, so the ingredient — most often fish, eggs, or fruit — cooks gently without falling apart.
glossary.usage: Ztracené vejce, ryba ve vývaru, hruška v koření a víně.

glossary.title: Confit
glossary.short_definition: Slow cooking an ingredient submerged in fat or oil at a low temperature.
glossary.detailed: Originally a way of preserving meat (most often duck) in its own fat; today the technique is also used for vegetables or garlic confited in olive oil.

glossary.title: Reduction
glossary.short_definition: Thickening a sauce or stock by simmering off liquid over gentle heat.
glossary.detailed: Longer simmering evaporates some of the water, concentrating the flavor and thickening the sauce without needing to add a roux or starch.

glossary.title: Sautéing
glossary.short_definition: Quick cooking in fat over high heat, with constant stirring or tossing.
glossary.detailed: Ingredients are cooked in a small amount of fat in a very hot pan so they stay juicy inside while lightly browning on the surface.

glossary.title: Gratin
glossary.short_definition: Browning a dish under the broiler or in the oven until it forms a crisp golden crust.
glossary.detailed: A dish topped with cheese, breadcrumbs, or béchamel is finished under top heat until a crisp crust forms on the surface.

glossary.title: Flambé
glossary.short_definition: Igniting alcohol added to a hot dish, burning off the spirit and leaving only the flavor.
glossary.detailed: Alcohol (brandy, rum, wine) is added to a hot pan and carefully lit — the flame burns off quickly, leaving the dish a concentrated flavor without a sharp alcoholic edge.

glossary.title: Emulsion
glossary.short_definition: The blending of two otherwise unmixable liquids, such as oil and water, into one smooth mixture.
glossary.detailed: Formed by dispersing one liquid into another through vigorous whisking, often with egg yolk as the emulsifier — mayonnaise and carbonara's sauce are classic examples.

glossary.title: Julienne
glossary.short_definition: Cutting vegetables into thin, evenly sized matchsticks.
glossary.detailed: Vegetables are cut into thin slices and then into thin strips a few centimeters long — used mainly for garnish and quick sautéing.

glossary.title: Grilling
glossary.short_definition: Cooking meat or vegetables directly over glowing charcoal or on a hot grate.
glossary.detailed: High, direct heat gives food its characteristic charred crust and smoky flavor — a key technique in both Balkan and Greek cooking.

glossary.title: Braising
glossary.short_definition: Slow-cooking meat or vegetables in a small amount of liquid under a lid.
glossary.detailed: The ingredient is first browned, then slowly simmered tender over gentle heat in liquid — stock, wine, or beer. An ideal technique for tougher cuts of meat.

glossary.title: Marinating
glossary.short_definition: Soaking meat or vegetables in a seasoned liquid before cooking.
glossary.detailed: A marinade (usually vinegar-, wine-, or yogurt-based) tenderizes meat and builds flavor before cooking even begins — for some recipes, it takes several days.

glossary.title: Proofing
glossary.short_definition: Letting yeasted dough rest in a warm spot until it rises.
glossary.detailed: Yeast or sourdough starter releases carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise. The dough rests in a warm place under a towel, usually once or even twice.

glossary.title: Roux
glossary.short_definition: A thickener made from flour toasted in fat, the base of many Central European sauces and soups.
glossary.detailed: Flour is toasted in butter or lard, stirred constantly, until pale or golden, then thinned with liquid — the darker the roux, the more pronounced its nutty flavor.

glossary.title: Pancetta
glossary.short_definition: Italian unsmoked bacon cured in salt and spices, dry-aged.
glossary.detailed: Unlike English bacon, pancetta is never smoked — it's simply salted, seasoned, and left to age. Sold sliced or rolled.
glossary.substitute: Uzená slanina nebo pancetta v nouzi nahradí guanciale, chuť je ale méně výrazná.

glossary.title: Parmigiano Reggiano
glossary.short_definition: A hard aged cheese made from cow's milk, a protected Italian product with a long tradition.
glossary.detailed: It ages for at least 12 months, often much longer, and only cheese made in a precisely defined area of northern Italy may carry the name.

glossary.title: Arborio rice
glossary.short_definition: A round-grain Italian rice high in starch, the base of risotto.
glossary.detailed: As it cooks, it releases starch that thickens risotto to a creamy consistency without any cream being added.

glossary.title: Chorizo
glossary.short_definition: A Spanish smoked sausage seasoned with paprika, sold both fresh and cured.
glossary.detailed: Smoked ground paprika (pimentón) gives the sausage its signature red color and smoky flavor. Used fresh in cooking as well as sliced as a cured meat.

glossary.title: Jamón serrano
glossary.short_definition: Spanish dry-cured ham aged in mountain regions, sliced paper-thin.
glossary.detailed: A pork leg is first salted, then aged for months to years in dry mountain air. Served raw, sliced thin.

glossary.title: Bacalhau (dried salt cod)
glossary.short_definition: Cod preserved with salt and dried, a staple of Portuguese cuisine.
glossary.detailed: Before cooking it must be soaked in cold water for several days to remove the excess salt. Portugal has hundreds of recipes built around it.

glossary.title: Feta
glossary.short_definition: A salty Greek cheese made from sheep's or goat's milk, aged in brine.
glossary.detailed: Under EU protected-designation rules, feta may only come from Greece. It crumbles but doesn't melt away, which makes it ideal for both salads and baking.

glossary.title: Bryndza
glossary.short_definition: A salty Slovak cheese made from sheep's milk, with a sharp, tangy flavor.
glossary.detailed: Made by blending curdled sheep's-milk cheese with salt into a soft, spreadable consistency. The base of bryndzové halušky and pirohy alike.

glossary.title: Crème fraîche
glossary.short_definition: A cultured cream with a higher fat content and a mildly tangy flavor.
glossary.detailed: Unlike regular sour cream, it can take higher heat without curdling, which makes it well suited to hot sauces.
glossary.substitute: Hustá zakysaná smetana s vyšším podílem tuku.

glossary.title: Dijon mustard
glossary.short_definition: A smooth French mustard made from mustard seeds and white wine, without vinegar.
glossary.detailed: Made from black or brown mustard seed and white wine or must, which makes it milder and less sharp than a classic vinegar-based mustard.

glossary.title: Polenta
glossary.short_definition: A cornmeal porridge made from coarse ground corn, Italy's counterpart to Romanian mămăligă.
glossary.detailed: Made by slowly stirring cornmeal into boiling salted water or stock until it thickens. Served soft, or set firm and grilled.

glossary.title: Saffron
glossary.short_definition: The world's most expensive spice, the dried stigmas of the saffron crocus, deep golden in color.
glossary.detailed: A single gram of saffron requires hand-picking stigmas from dozens of flowers. Gives rice and sauces a characteristic golden color and a faintly bitter flavor.

glossary.title: Capers
glossary.short_definition: The pickled buds of the caper bush, a salty, sour addition to sauces and salads.
glossary.detailed: Picked while still closed buds and cured in vinegar or salt. A small amount adds a pronounced salty tang to a dish.

glossary.title: Prosciutto
glossary.short_definition: Italian dry-cured ham, the best known being prosciutto di Parma.
glossary.detailed: A pork leg is salted and left to age for at least a year. Served raw, sliced thin, often with melon or figs.

glossary.title: Ground paprika
glossary.short_definition: Dried, ground paprika, the essential spice of Hungarian cooking — both sweet and hot.
glossary.detailed: The best ground paprika comes from around the towns of Kalocsa and Szeged. It's always added off the heat, or it turns slightly bitter.

glossary.title: Olive oil
glossary.short_definition: The essential fat of Mediterranean cooking, pressed from ripe olives.
glossary.detailed: The best is extra virgin olive oil from the first cold pressing — it has the most pronounced flavor and the lowest acidity.

glossary.title: Bulgarian yogurt
glossary.short_definition: A thick cultured milk with a pronounced tang, linked to the bacterium Lactobacillus bulgaricus.
glossary.detailed: The lactic-fermentation bacterium used to make it is named directly after Bulgaria, where a Bulgarian microbiologist first described it in the early 20th century.

glossary.title: Antipasto
glossary.short_definition: An Italian cold starter served before the main course — cured meats, cheeses, vegetables.
glossary.detailed: Literally "before the meal." Typically a plate of prosciutto, olives, marinated vegetables, and a bit of cheese to open the appetite.

glossary.title: Aperitivo
glossary.short_definition: The Italian ritual of a pre-dinner drink with light snacks.
glossary.detailed: Usually between 6 and 8 p.m., when Italians have a light alcoholic drink (an Aperol Spritz, say) with small bites to wake up the appetite before dinner.

glossary.title: Digestif
glossary.short_definition: An alcoholic drink served after a meal, said to aid digestion.
glossary.detailed: Usually a stronger spirit — an herbal liqueur, brandy, or grappa — served in a small glass at the end of a meal.

glossary.title: Tapas
glossary.short_definition: Small Spanish dishes meant for sharing, usually served with wine or beer.
glossary.detailed: From simple olives to elaborate hot dishes — several kinds of tapas are ordered at once and shared around the table.

glossary.title: Meze
glossary.short_definition: A shared spread of small cold and hot starters, typical of Greece and the Balkans.
glossary.detailed: Similar to tapas, it's a way of eating — several small dishes arrive at the table at once, and everyone shares from them together.

glossary.title: Terroir
glossary.short_definition: The sum of a place's soil, climate, and tradition, which stamps a characteristic flavor onto wine and food.
glossary.detailed: A term from French winemaking, now also applied to ingredients in general — the same variety grown elsewhere tastes different.

glossary.title: Protected Designation of Origin (PDO/PGI)
glossary.short_definition: An EU system that protects a food name tied to a specific region and traditional method of production.
glossary.detailed: Marked with the abbreviations PDO (Protected Designation of Origin) and PGI (Protected Geographical Indication) — Parmigiano Reggiano or kranjska klobasa, for instance, may only carry their name if made to the specified recipe and in the specified place.

glossary.title: Fika
glossary.short_definition: The Swedish ritual of an afternoon coffee break with something sweet, usually a cinnamon bun.
glossary.detailed: Fika isn't just a snack but a social pause — at Swedish workplaces it's often even a fixed part of the daily schedule.

glossary.title: Mise en place
glossary.short_definition: Prepping and laying out every ingredient and tool in advance, before cooking begins.
glossary.detailed: Literally "put in place." A basic rule of professional kitchens — everything chopped, measured, and set out in bowls so the cooking itself runs smoothly.

glossary.title: Degustation
glossary.short_definition: A tasting of a larger number of smaller portions of food or wine to assess flavor.
glossary.detailed: In restaurants, a degustation menu is made up of several small courses so a guest tastes as wide a range of the kitchen's flavors as possible.

glossary.title: Smörgåsbord
glossary.short_definition: The Swedish style of dining as a lavish cold-and-hot buffet.
glossary.detailed: Traditionally eaten in a set order — from fish, through cold meats, to hot dishes and cheese at the end.

glossary.title: Paellera
glossary.short_definition: A wide, shallow two-handled pan traditionally used to cook paella.
glossary.detailed: Its large diameter and shallow depth mean the rice cooks in a thin layer, letting the prized crispy socarrat layer form on the bottom.

glossary.title: Mandoline
glossary.short_definition: A kitchen slicing tool for thin, even slices or strips of vegetables.
glossary.detailed: Lets you cut vegetables into thin, even slices quickly — something a hand knife can rarely match for precision.

glossary.title: Mortar and pestle
glossary.short_definition: A bowl and pounder for crushing spices, garlic, or herbs.
glossary.detailed: Crushing, rather than chopping, releases more of an ingredient's oils and flavor — tzatziki or pesto are traditionally made this way.

glossary.title: Dutch oven
glossary.short_definition: A heavy cast-iron pot with a lid, ideal for long braising on the stovetop or in the oven.
glossary.detailed: Thick walls hold a steady temperature through long braising, so the food never scorches and softens evenly.

glossary.title: Kitchen thermometer
glossary.short_definition: A tool for measuring the internal temperature of meat to hit the exact doneness.
glossary.detailed: Especially with large cuts like beef Wellington, an insta-read thermometer is the only reliable way to hit the target doneness.

glossary.title: Springform pan
glossary.short_definition: A round baking pan with a side latch that opens after baking for easy release of the cake.
glossary.detailed: Indispensable for moist or layered cakes like Sachertorte or Dobos torta, which would be nearly impossible to turn out whole from a regular pan.
